readings.title: Black Beauty: My Early Home (Chapter I)
readings.challenge: Listen to the narrator’s voice and decide what kind of storyteller a horse can be.
readings.focus: The first chapter sets up the whole book: a mother’s advice, a kind master, and a boy who is cruel for fun.
readings.context: Black Beauty (1877) is the only book by the English writer Anna Sewell, who wrote it during her last years of illness and died a few months after it was published. A horse tells his own life story, and Sewell meant it to make people kinder to horses, which in her time pulled almost every cart, cab and carriage. The edition here is the first one; its title page calls the book “Translated from the Original Equine” (equine means “of horses”), a joke that asks readers to imagine a horse really wrote it. A colt is a young male horse; a gig is a light two-wheeled cart. Sewell uses older British spellings and words such as “whilst” (while).

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “My Early Home,” the whole chapter; opens “The first place that I can well remember, was a large pleasant meadow with a pond of…”; closes “…man who looked after the horses, was just as gentle as our master, so we were well off.”.

questions.prompt: Who is telling this story? Find two details that only a horse could tell.
facilitatorNotes: The colt himself, later named Black Beauty. He lived on his mother’s milk because he “could not eat grass,” runs with the colts, and is called “Darkie” for his dull black coat. Ask what a horse narrator can notice that a person might not.
evidence: Whilst I was young I lived upon my mother's milk, as I could not eat grass.
I was a dull black, so he called me Darkie

questions.prompt: What does Duchess want her son to become? Why does she say the other colts “have not learned manners”?
facilitatorNotes: Gentle and good, a willing worker who never bites or kicks, “even in play.” She points to his family to say he was born to better behaviour than the cart-horse colts. Readers may question whether good manners really depend on birth; the book will test her advice many times.
evidence: they have not learned manners
never bite or kick even in play

questions.prompt: Compare how the master treats the horses with how Dick treats them.
facilitatorNotes: The master gives “good food, good lodging, and kind words” and speaks to them as to his own children; Dick throws stones for “fun.” The narrator’s phrase “what he called, fun” shows he disagrees with Dick’s word.
evidence: good food, good lodging, and kind words
he would have, what he called, fun with the colts

questions.prompt: Was the master right to dismiss Dick and box his ear? Use the text to explain your view.
facilitatorNotes: He catches Dick in the act and says it is not the first time. Some readers will think losing his job was fair; others may notice that the master answers cruelty with a blow. Both views can use the text; the narrator simply says “we were well off.”
evidence: This is not the first time, nor the second, but it shall be the last
so we were well off

readings.title: Black Beauty: The Hunt (Chapter II)
readings.challenge: Notice the difference between what the narrator saw and what he heard about afterwards.
readings.focus: A morning’s sport ends in three deaths, and the old mare asks whether it was worth it.
readings.context: Recap: the young colt lives in a meadow with his wise mother, Duchess, and a kind master who sent away a boy for throwing stones at the horses. In a hunt, riders on horseback follow a pack of hounds chasing a hare, fox or deer; a squire is the chief landowner of a village; a farrier shoes and treats horses.
readings.contentNote: Hounds kill a hare; a young rider dies when his horse falls; the injured horse is shot; the chapter ends with a funeral.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “The Hunt,” the whole chapter; opens “Before I was two years old, a circumstance happened, which I have never forgotten. It was…”; closes “…ride again. What they did with Rob Roy I never knew; but 'twas all for one little hare.”.

questions.prompt: How does the colt describe the hounds and the riders? What words show he is seeing a hunt for the first time?
facilitatorNotes: He hears “what sounded like the cry of dogs,” says he “never heard such a noise,” and copies their “yo! yo, o, o!” The older horses “seemed to know all about it.” Ask how the scene would read if a hunter told it.
evidence: I never heard such a noise as they made.
seemed to know all about it

questions.prompt: When the rider is killed, one colt says, “And serve him right too.” What does Duchess answer, and why does she disagree?
facilitatorNotes: She says “you must not say that,” yet questions the sport itself: men hurt themselves and spoil horses “all for a hare.” She judges the sport, not the young man. Ask readers whether that is a fair difference.
evidence: you must not say that
I never yet could make out why men are so fond of this sport

questions.prompt: The last sentence is “'twas all for one little hare.” What is the narrator saying by ending this way?
facilitatorNotes: Three lives — the hare, George Gordon and Rob Roy — are set against what the hunt was for. The short final phrase turns a description into a judgment. Readers can say whether they agree.
evidence: 'twas all for one little hare

questions.prompt: How do sounds change through the chapter, from the hunt’s noise to the end?
facilitatorNotes: The hounds’ loud cry; one shriek from the hare; “There was no noise now”; the gun and a “dreadful shriek”; then the church bell “tolling, tolling.” Sound tracks the change from excitement to grief.
evidence: There was no noise now
while the bell kept tolling, tolling

readings.title: Black Beauty: bit, saddle and shoes (Chapter III, first part)
readings.challenge: Follow a process in order and notice how the narrator feels about each step.
readings.focus: Breaking in means learning to do another’s will; the master makes it bearable by patience.
readings.context: Recap: after a hunt in which a young man and a fine horse were killed, the narrator learned that his mother never understood why men loved the sport. He is now growing up. “Breaking in” is training a young horse to be ridden or to pull a vehicle. A crupper and breeching are straps of harness; a chaise is a light carriage; a smith or blacksmith makes and fits iron shoes.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “My Breaking In,” from the start through the new iron shoes; opens “I was now beginning to grow handsome; my coat had grown fine and soft, and was bright…”; closes “…the shoe was firmly on. My feet felt very stiff and heavy, but in time I got used to it.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the master refuse to sell the colt until he is four? What does this show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He says lads should not work like men and colts should not work like horses until they are grown. He puts the young horse’s health before an early sale.
evidence: lads ought not to work like men, and colts ought not to work like horses till they were quite grown up

questions.prompt: The narrator says a broken-in horse may not “have any will of his own.” Which line about harness seems hardest to him, and why?
facilitatorNotes: “He may neither jump for joy nor lie down for weariness”: a horse in harness cannot express feeling at all. The list of “nor” clauses builds up all he must give up. Ask what “So you will see this breaking in is a great thing” means here.
evidence: nor have any will of his own
he may neither jump for joy nor lie down for weariness

questions.prompt: How does the narrator make the bit real for a reader who has never worn one?
facilitatorNotes: He describes it from inside: cold hard steel as thick as a finger, pushed over the tongue and held with straps, “no way in the world can you get rid of” it. He even says “one’s mouth” and “your mouth,” putting the reader in his place.
evidence: a great piece of cold hard steel as thick as a man's finger
it is very bad! yes, very bad!

questions.prompt: What helps the colt accept the bit and the saddle?
facilitatorNotes: Oats, pats, kind words, gentle ways, and doing a little every day; also seeing his mother wear a bit. The master trains by patience and reward, which later chapters will contrast with force.
evidence: what with the nice oats, and what with my master's pats, kind words, and gentle ways
this he did every day till I began to look for the oats and the saddle

readings.title: Black Beauty: blinkers, trains and a mother’s warning (Chapter III, end)
readings.challenge: Find the lesson the narrator draws, and decide whether he has earned it from what happened.
readings.focus: A frightening train becomes ordinary, and Duchess warns that a horse’s life depends on the people who own him.
readings.context: Recap: the master has taught the colt to wear a bit, a saddle and iron shoes, gently and a little at a time. Blinkers are leather flaps beside a horse’s eyes; pales are fence posts; a fortnight is two weeks. Railways were still fairly new in the English countryside when the story is set.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “My Breaking In,” from the harness and blinkers to the end of the chapter; opens “And now having got so far, my master went on to break me to harness; there were more new…”; closes “…chance for us, but still I say, do your best wherever it is, and keep up your good name."”.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator describe his first train? Why doesn’t he call it a train at first?
facilitatorNotes: “A long black train of something flew by”: he has no name for it yet, so he describes its rush, clatter and smoke, and calls it a “terrible creature.” The words show what it looked like to a young horse.
evidence: a long black train of something flew by
this terrible creature never came into the field

questions.prompt: What changed his fear, and what does the cows’ behaviour have to do with it?
facilitatorNotes: The cows hardly raised their heads, and the train never came into the field or hurt him; within days he cared “as little” as they did. He learned by watching calm animals and by experience.
evidence: the cows went on eating very quietly
I cared as little about the passing of a train, as the cows and sheep did

questions.prompt: Duchess names three kinds of men. Which kind does she say does the most harm, and why is that surprising?
facilitatorNotes: The foolish, vain and careless, who “spoil more horses than all” though “they don't mean it.” It is surprising because one expects cruel men to do the most harm. Ask readers for an example of harm done by not thinking.
evidence: these spoil more horses than all, just for want of sense
they don't mean it, but they do it for all that

questions.prompt: “It is all a chance for us.” What does Duchess mean, and what does she advise her son to do about it?
facilitatorNotes: A horse cannot choose who buys or drives him. She advises him to do his best wherever he is and “keep up your good name.” Readers can predict how this advice will be tested.
evidence: a horse never knows who may buy him, or who may drive him; it is all a chance for us
keep up your good name

readings.title: Black Beauty: Birtwick Park (Chapter IV)
readings.challenge: Make a first impression of two new characters, and look for clues that it may change.
readings.focus: The narrator moves to a new home and meets Merrylegs, who is cheerful, and Ginger, who bites.
readings.context: Recap: the master trained the colt with patience, and his mother warned him that a horse never knows who will own him. Now Squire Gordon, the squire whose son died in the hunt, has bought him. A lodge is a small house at the gate of an estate; a paddock is a small field; a loose box is a stall where the horse is not tied up; corn here means oats or other grain.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Birtwick Park,” the whole chapter; opens “At this time I used to stand in the stable, and my coat was brushed every day till it…”; closes “…boy as James is, so that it is all Ginger's own fault that she did not stay in that box."”.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator say goodbye to his first master, and how does he feel about leaving?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot speak, so he puts his nose in the master’s hand. He says little about feelings, but the gesture shows them. Ask readers what “I left my first home” suggests.
evidence: I could not say 'good bye,' so I put my nose into his hand
and I left my first home

questions.prompt: Why does Ginger greet him rudely? Is her complaint fair?
facilitatorNotes: He has been put in her old loose box, and she calls him a “colt.” He replies he had nothing to do with it and is grown-up. Her complaint is aimed at the wrong horse, but readers may sympathise with losing a home.
evidence: So it is you who have turned me out of my box
I had nothing to do with it

questions.prompt: What does Merrylegs say about why Ginger bites? Do you believe him?
facilitatorNotes: He says it is “just a bad habit,” but adds that she “must have been very ill-used.” Then he decides it is “all Ginger's own fault.” His explanation contradicts itself; ask readers to notice this and predict what Ginger’s own story will be.
evidence: she must have been very ill-used before she came here
it is all Ginger's own fault

questions.prompt: What kind of character is Merrylegs, judging by how he talks?
facilitatorNotes: Proud and chatty (“I am very handsome”), fond of the girls, and sure he knows best because he is twelve. His “wise look” is a little funny. Ask for a word to describe him and a line that proves it.
evidence: I am very handsome
I am twelve years old; I know a great deal

readings.title: Black Beauty: A Fair Start (Chapter V)
readings.challenge: Watch how a name is chosen, and notice what a casual conversation suddenly reveals.
readings.focus: The horse receives his name, and learns by chance that Rob Roy, killed in the hunt, was his brother.
readings.context: Recap: the narrator has come to Birtwick Park, where he shares a stable with friendly Merrylegs and bad-tempered Ginger. John Manly is the coachman (who drives and cares for the carriage horses) and James Howard the stable boy. A common is open land anyone may use; Marengo, Pegasus and Abdallah were names of famous horses.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “A Fair Start,” the whole chapter; opens “The name of the coachman was John Manly; he had a wife and one little child, and they…”; closes “…course I could not be so intimate with him as with Ginger, who stood in the same stable.”.

questions.prompt: What does John notice on the first ride, and what does he conclude about the horse’s past?
facilitatorNotes: He passes a cart hung with baskets without fuss and stands still when a gun goes off. John concludes he “has not been frightened or ill-used” when young. Connect to the patient breaking in of Chapter III.
evidence: he just took a good look at it, and then went on as quiet and pleasant as could be
he has not been frightened or ill-used while he was young

questions.prompt: How do the Squire and his wife choose a name? Why do they turn down “Ebony” and “Blackbird”?
facilitatorNotes: They reject names that only describe colour or belong to another horse, and choose one that matches his “good-tempered face” and “intelligent eye.” Ask what the name says about how they see him.
evidence: he is really quite a beauty
what do you say to calling him 'Black Beauty?'

questions.prompt: What does the narrator learn about Rob Roy? How does this change the hunt in Chapter II?
facilitatorNotes: Rob Roy was his brother; both were sons of Duchess. He understands now why his mother “was so troubled.” The hunt’s loss becomes personal, and the reader rereads the earlier chapter.
evidence: poor Rob Roy who was killed at that hunt was my brother!
I did not wonder that my mother was so troubled.

questions.prompt: “It seems that horses have no relations.” What does the narrator mean, and how does it make you feel?
facilitatorNotes: Horses are sold away from their families and never know each other afterwards. A plain sentence states something sad about horses’ lives; readers may compare it with how people stay in touch.
evidence: It seems that horses have no relations; at least, they never know each other after they are sold.

readings.title: Black Beauty: Liberty, and Ginger’s breaking in (Chapters VI and VII, first part)
readings.challenge: Compare two horses’ upbringings and look for the reasons they turned out differently.
readings.focus: The narrator misses freedom even in a good home; then Ginger explains why she has never trusted anyone.
readings.context: Recap: John found the horse calm and well trained, and the Squire’s wife named him Black Beauty. He has learned that Rob Roy, killed in the hunt, was his brother. Skittish means easily excited; to be weaned is to stop drinking a mother’s milk; a halter is a rope or strap for leading a horse.
readings.contentNote: Ginger describes being caught and forced into a halter and bit, with flogging.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “Liberty,” whole, and Chapter VII, “Ginger,” through her account of her breaking in; opens “I was quite happy in my new place, and if there was one thing that I missed, it must not…”; closes “…you have a kind master and plenty of coaxing, but there was nothing of that sort for me.”.

questions.prompt: “Why, liberty!” What does Black Beauty miss, even though his home is good?
facilitatorNotes: Space to gallop and fling up his head, after three and a half years in a field; now he stands in a stable and wears straps, bit and blinkers. He insists he is “not complaining,” yet says it is hard. Ask whether one can be well treated and still unfree.
evidence: Why, liberty!
Now, I am not complaining, for I know it must be so.

questions.prompt: How does John deal with the horse’s high spirits? What would some other grooms do?
facilitatorNotes: He gives him a fast trot to clear “the fidgets,” and uses his voice, while “some grooms will punish” such play. John understands it is only high spirits.
evidence: some grooms will punish them, but our John did not
he knew it was only high spirits

questions.prompt: List three ways Ginger’s early life was different from Black Beauty’s.
facilitatorNotes: Taken from her mother as soon as weaned; no kind master or kind word; boys threw stones; breaking in done “all force.” Black Beauty had his mother, a kind master and gentle training. Readers can use this to test Merrylegs’s claim that biting is “Ginger’s own fault.”
evidence: I was taken from my mother as soon as I was weaned
it was all force; they did not give me a chance to know what they wanted

questions.prompt: Ginger says, “if I had had your bringing up I might have been as good a temper as you are.” Do you agree that upbringing makes temper?
facilitatorNotes: Her story supports the idea: no kindness, then force. She also admits she was “very wild” and gave trouble. Readers may argue both upbringing and nature matter; ask for evidence from both horses’ stories.
evidence: if I had had your bringing up I might have been as good a temper as you are
was very wild, no doubt

readings.title: Black Beauty: Samson and the old master (Chapter VII, end)
readings.challenge: Compare two trainers in the same story, and find the sentence that sums up the difference.
readings.focus: Ginger’s story reaches its worst moment, and one kind old man shows what could have been.
readings.context: Recap: Ginger has told Black Beauty that she was taken from her mother young, never had a kind word, and was broken in by force. A sieve is a shallow wire-bottomed container; a bran mash is warm soft food; a filly is a young female horse; spurs are spikes on a rider’s heels.
readings.contentNote: Ginger is whipped and spurred until she bleeds; the trainer drinks heavily.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “Ginger,” from “There was one—the old master” to the end of the chapter; opens “"There was one—the old master, Mr Ryder, who I think could soon have brought me round,…”; closes “…went on training me; he was steady and thoughtful, and I soon learned what he wanted."”.

questions.prompt: How does Ginger describe Samson? What does the repeated word “hard” do?
facilitatorNotes: “A hard voice, a hard eye, a hard hand”: the repetition makes him seem made of hardness. He wanted to wear the spirit out of her and make her mere “horse-flesh.”
evidence: a hard voice, a hard eye, a hard hand
a quiet, humble, obedient piece of horse-flesh

questions.prompt: How did the fight on the training ground begin, and who does Ginger blame?
facilitatorNotes: She was exhausted and given a painful new bit; Samson “chucked” the rein, she reared, he flogged her, and she threw him. She admits “something I did put him out of temper,” but shows how hard treatment pushed her to fight. Ask whether she was wrong to fight.
evidence: I could never quite tell how it came about
I began to kick, and plunge, and rear as I had never done before

questions.prompt: What does the old master do differently? Find the words he says to Samson.
facilitatorNotes: He comes at sunset with oats and a calm voice, washes her wounds and orders soft food. He tells Samson, “a bad-tempered man will never make a good-tempered horse.” Compare his voice, “full, and clear, and kind,” with Samson’s.
evidence: his voice took all my fear away
a bad-tempered man will never make a good-tempered horse

questions.prompt: Why does the old master’s kindness matter so much to the story, when he appears for only one evening?
facilitatorNotes: It proves Ginger could have been gentle; she trusted him at once, and later Job trained her “steady and thoughtful.” It also prepares readers to hope she may improve at Birtwick.
evidence: I stood still and let him come up
he was steady and thoughtful, and I soon learned what he wanted

readings.title: Black Beauty: Ginger’s Story Continued (Chapter VIII)
readings.challenge: Follow a chain of causes from one place to the next, and notice how kindness breaks the chain.
readings.focus: The bearing rein, fashion and harsh grooms made Ginger fight; at Birtwick, patience begins to cure her.
readings.context: Recap: Ginger has told how she was broken in by force, fought the cruel trainer Samson, and was comforted by his kind father. A bearing rein is a strap that holds a horse’s head high, used then mostly for looks; Tattersall’s (Sewell spells it “Tattersal's”) was a famous London horse auction; a turn-out is a carriage and horses; horse-balls were pills given to horses.
readings.contentNote: Ginger describes a sharp bit making her mouth bleed, beatings with a broom and a whip, and pain from the bearing rein.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “Ginger's Story Continued,” the whole chapter; opens “The next time that Ginger and I were together in the paddock, she told me about her first…”; closes “…each to be mixed up with half-a-pint of common sense, and given to the horse every day.”.

questions.prompt: Why did Ginger’s master in London use a tight bearing rein? What did it do to her?
facilitatorNotes: He and his coachman thought horses “looked more stylish so.” It forced her head up for hours, her neck ached, the sharp bit made her tongue bleed, and it hurt her breathing. Fashion matters more to him than pain.
evidence: thinking we looked more stylish so
the blood from my tongue coloured the froth

questions.prompt: “What right had they to make me suffer like that?” How would you answer Ginger?
facilitatorNotes: She was willing to work hard but not to be “tormented for nothing but their fancies.” Readers can discuss what people owe animals that work for them.
evidence: I was willing to work, and ready to work hard too
What right had they to make me suffer like that?

questions.prompt: Trace how Ginger came to believe men were her “natural enemies.” What happened at each place?
facilitatorNotes: Bearing rein and blows in London; a rough groom who hit her with a broom; sold each time she fought back. Each harsh place made her more defensive, so she decided she must defend herself.
evidence: men were my natural enemies, and that I must defend myself
he would hit me above the hocks with the stable broom

questions.prompt: What are “the Birtwick balls,” and why is it a joke?
facilitatorNotes: Not real medicine: patience, gentleness, firmness and petting, mixed with common sense. John jokes in a recipe’s words, but the change in Ginger is real; she even whinnies after James.
evidence: made up of patience and gentleness, firmness and petting
kindness is all the physic she wants

readings.title: Black Beauty: Merrylegs (Chapter IX)
readings.challenge: Hear both sides of a quarrel and decide whether a character’s actions match his words.
readings.focus: Merrylegs gives some rough boys a lesson, and explains why a good place makes a good horse.
readings.context: Recap of Chapters I–VIII: Black Beauty grew up with his mother and a kind master, was gently broken in, and was sold to Squire Gordon of Birtwick Park. There he works with Ginger, a chestnut mare made fierce by cruel treatment who is slowly becoming gentle, and lives beside Merrylegs, a fat grey pony who carries the Squire’s daughters. John Manly is the coachman and James the stable boy. A vicar is a parish priest; a drover drives cattle to market.
readings.contentNote: Merrylegs repeats a groom’s remark that big sticks are fit only for “drovers or gipsies,” an insulting phrase about the Romani people that was common at the time.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “Merrylegs,” the whole chapter; opens “Mr. Blomefield, the Vicar, had a large family of boys and girls; sometimes they used to…”; closes “…before I came here; no," said he, shaking his head, "I hope I shall never come to that."”.

questions.prompt: What did Merrylegs do to the boys, and why? Find his own explanation.
facilitatorNotes: After an hour of being whipped with hazel sticks he stopped as a hint, then let each boy slip off behind. He says boys think a pony is like a steam engine and never think it can get tired.
evidence: I stopped two or three times by way of a hint
they never think that a pony can get tired, or have any feelings

questions.prompt: How does Merrylegs treat the little children differently from the boys? Why?
facilitatorNotes: He goes “smooth and as quiet as old pussy” when they are frightened and speeds up only as they grow confident. They are in his charge; the boys were misusing him.
evidence: I go as smooth and as quiet as old pussy when she is after a bird
those children are under my charge when they are riding

questions.prompt: Ginger would have kicked the boys. Why does Merrylegs refuse?
facilitatorNotes: He will not anger the master or shame James; he is trusted and loves his people; and a kicking pony could be sold to a hard life. Ask readers which reason seems strongest.
evidence: I am not quite such a fool, (begging your pardon) as to anger our master
I love them, I do

questions.prompt: “Good places make good horses.” How does Merrylegs’s life support this? How does Ginger’s?
facilitatorNotes: Five years of kind treatment make Merrylegs trustworthy; Ginger, who “never had a good place,” learned to fight. Both stories point the same way, which is the book’s main argument.
evidence: good places make good horses
you never had a good place where they were kind to you

readings.title: Black Beauty: a light hand and Sir Oliver’s tail (Chapter X, first part)
readings.challenge: Find the word that the characters keep returning to, and decide whether they are right.
readings.focus: An old horse’s story about his docked tail leads to an angry argument against fashion.
readings.context: Recap: Merrylegs threw some rough boys who whipped him but would never kick, because good places make good horses. A hand is four inches, used to measure horses; docking is cutting off part of a tail; a terrier is a small dog; a gag bit is a severe bit; “forsooth” is an old word that mocks what came before it.
readings.contentNote: Sir Oliver describes his tail being cut off and a litter of puppies having their tails and ears cut; he mentions that puppies of less valuable kinds were drowned.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, “A Talk in the Orchard,” from the start through the narrator’s bitter feeling toward men; opens “Ginger and I were not of the regular tall carriage horse breed, we had more of the racing…”; closes “…eyes, and distended nostrils, declaring that men were both brutes and blockheads.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Black Beauty prefer carrying the mistress? What does that teach about riders?
facilitatorNotes: Her hand is so light on the rein he is guided almost without feeling it. A light hand keeps a good mouth and good temper; people who “chuck, and drag, and pull” spoil it.
evidence: her hand was so light on the rein, that I was guided almost without feeling it
they surely would not chuck, and drag, and pull at the rein as they often do

questions.prompt: Sir Oliver says losing his tail was “a life-long wrong.” What were the two kinds of harm?
facilitatorNotes: The pain, and the loss of his “best ornament,” but worst of all he can no longer brush flies away. He thinks of daily life, not looks. Notice his relief that “they don't do it now.”
evidence: how could I ever brush the flies off my sides and my hind legs any more?
a life-long wrong, and a life-long loss

questions.prompt: What does Sir Oliver blame, and what example does he give from dogs?
facilitatorNotes: “Fashion,” “one of the wickedest things in the world”: a terrier’s puppies came back with tails and ears cut so they would look “plucky” and “sharp.” He asks why people don’t cut their own children’s ears the same way.
evidence: fashion is one of the wickedest things in the world
What right have they to torment and disfigure God's creatures?

questions.prompt: How does the story change Black Beauty’s feelings? Is that a fair reaction?
facilitatorNotes: For the first time he feels “a bitter feeling toward men.” Ginger calls men “brutes and blockheads.” Readers can discuss whether one story should change how we see everyone, and what the next part of the chapter says.
evidence: I found a bitter feeling toward men rise up in my mind that I never had before

readings.title: Black Beauty: the use of blinkers (Chapter X, end)
readings.challenge: Follow an argument where each speaker gives a reason, and decide which reason is strongest.
readings.focus: The horses debate blinkers, and Merrylegs keeps a bitter talk from turning unfair.
readings.context: Recap: old Sir Oliver told how fashion made people cut off his tail and crop puppies’ ears, and the horses grew angry with all men. Blinkers are leather flaps beside a horse’s eyes; Justice is a calm roan cob (a sturdy horse); a hearse carries a coffin; shying is jumping aside in fright.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, “A Talk in the Orchard,” from Merrylegs’s “Who talks about blockheads?” to the end of the chapter; opens “"Who talks about blockheads?" said Merrylegs, who just came up from the old apple tree,…”; closes “…got up our spirits by munching some very sweet apples which lay scattered on the grass.”.

questions.prompt: How does Merrylegs calm the others down? Was he right to?
facilitatorNotes: He says talk against men “in such a place as this” is not fair or grateful, since their own people are good. Readers can discuss whether he is being fair, or avoiding a real wrong; he admits “It is all true.”
evidence: It is all true
talking against men in such a place as this, doesn't seem fair or grateful

questions.prompt: What is the case for blinkers, and the case against? Who makes each?
facilitatorNotes: Justice gives the reason people use them: to stop shying and accidents. Then he and Sir Oliver argue: riding horses go without them; seeing “bits of things” is more frightening; and at night they hide dangers horses could see.
evidence: to prevent horses from shying and starting
be much less frightened than by only seeing bits of things

questions.prompt: What evidence does Sir Oliver give that blinkers cause accidents?
facilitatorNotes: The hearse that overturned into a pond, drowning both horses, and the master’s overturned carriage, when old Colin would have seen the hole “lamp or no lamp.” Ask whether two examples prove the point.
evidence: the hearse was overturned into the water
he would have seen it, lamp or no lamp

questions.prompt: How is Ginger’s remark about eyes “in the middle of their foreheads” funny, and what is her real point?
facilitatorNotes: It is sarcasm: if men think they can improve on nature, they should redesign horses entirely. Her point is that blinkers try to correct how God made horses, and make things worse.
evidence: all foals should be born with their eyes set just in the middle of their foreheads
they always think they can improve upon nature and mend what God has made

readings.title: Black Beauty: Plain Speaking (Chapter XI)
readings.challenge: Compare how one man speaks to two very different people about the same kind of wrong.
readings.focus: The Squire speaks out against cruelty, sternly to a builder and with a joke to a friend.
readings.context: Recap: in the orchard the horses argued about docked tails and blinkers, and Merrylegs reminded them that their own people are kind. Captain Langley addresses Squire Gordon as “Mr. Douglas.” A pony chaise is a small carriage; a break is a large open carriage used for training horses; a backboard is a board strapped to a person’s back to force an upright posture; a hobby here means a favourite subject.
readings.contentNote: A man lashes a small pony and nearly breaks its jaw.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, “Plain Speaking,” the whole chapter; opens “The longer I lived at Birtwick, the more proud and happy I felt at having such a place.…”; closes “…rather a hard hit about the soldiers; but—well—I'll think about it," and so they parted.”.

questions.prompt: What did the master and mistress do when they saw a creature ill-used?
facilitatorNotes: “There was no oppressed or ill-used creature that had not a friend in them”; the mistress would get out and “reason with the driver.” Ask what “plain speaking” means in the title.
evidence: there was no oppressed or ill-used creature that had not a friend in them
reason with the driver in her sweet serious voice

questions.prompt: How does the Squire speak to Sawyer? What reason does Sawyer give, and how does the Squire answer it?
facilitatorNotes: Sawyer says the pony “had no business to make that turn.” The Squire says the turn only shows the creature’s memory and intelligence, and that brutality injures Sawyer’s character more than the horse.
evidence: is that pony made of flesh and blood?
you injure your own character as much, nay more, than you injure your horse

questions.prompt: What comparison does the Squire use to persuade Captain Langley? Why might it work on a soldier?
facilitatorNotes: Soldiers with heads tied to a backboard could not fight in a bayonet charge; horses held up by bearing reins cannot pull with all their strength. He speaks Langley’s own language.
evidence: if all your men had their heads tied to a backboard
horses were intended to have their heads free, as free as men's are

questions.prompt: Compare the two conversations. Why is the Squire stern with one man and joking with the other? Which approach might work better?
facilitatorNotes: Sawyer’s cruelty is open and furious; Langley’s is fashion and habit. The Squire laughs about his “hobby” but still asks for an example. Langley only says “I'll think about it.” Readers can debate which approach changes minds.
evidence: I have given my hobby a good trot out
I'll think about it

readings.title: Black Beauty: A Stormy Day (Chapter XII)
readings.challenge: Track the danger as it builds, and notice the moment when a horse knows more than his driver.
readings.focus: On a stormy night Black Beauty refuses to cross a bridge, and saves his master and John.
readings.context: Recap: the Squire speaks out against cruelty to horses, both to a cruel builder and to a friend who uses bearing reins. A dog-cart is a light two-wheeled cart; a toll-bar is a gate where travellers paid to use the road; to give a horse a bait is to feed him on a journey.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, “A Stormy Day,” the whole chapter; opens “One day late in the autumn, my master had a long journey to go on business. I was put…”; closes “…beans with my oats, and such a thick bed of straw, and I was glad of it, for I was tired.”.

questions.prompt: Find three warnings before the bridge. How does the writer build up danger?
facilitatorNotes: The river “rising fast,” flooded meadows, the wind getting higher, then the oak falling “just before us.” Each warning is bigger, so the reader is ready to fear the bridge.
evidence: the river was rising fast
came an oak, torn up by the roots

questions.prompt: Why does Black Beauty stop on the bridge, even when he is whipped?
facilitatorNotes: He “felt sure there was something wrong” the moment his feet touched it. He cannot explain; he only knows. The master’s whip shows that even good people can be wrong.
evidence: I felt sure there was something wrong
I knew very well that the bridge was not safe

questions.prompt: What does the master say about how men and animals know things?
facilitatorNotes: Men have reason; animals have a knowledge “which did not depend on reason,” quicker and more perfect in its way, which has often saved lives. Ask whether readers agree, with an example.
evidence: He had given animals knowledge which did not depend on reason
by which they had often saved the lives of men

questions.prompt: How does the chapter end, and why might Sewell end with a good supper?
facilitatorNotes: The mistress’s fear and the master’s words “if your Black Beauty had not been wiser than we were”; then John’s thanks in a mash, beans, oats and deep straw. Kindness is shown, not said.
evidence: if your Black Beauty had not been wiser than we were
Oh! what a good supper he gave me that night

readings.title: Black Beauty: The Devil’s Trade Mark (Chapter XIII)
readings.challenge: Connect two stories about the same boy and find the lesson that joins them.
readings.focus: A cruel boy is thrown into a hedge, and James remembers a schoolmaster’s lesson about cruelty.
readings.context: Recap: Black Beauty refused to cross a broken bridge in a storm and saved his master and John. A quickset hedge is a thick hedge of hawthorn; “it roiles me” is country speech for “it angers me”; a trade mark is a sign that shows who made something.
readings.contentNote: A boy beats a pony and pulls the wings off flies; James hits the boy hard. The chapter speaks of God and the Devil.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIII, “The Devil's Trade Mark,” the whole chapter; opens “One day when John and I had been out on some business of our master's, and were returning…”; closes “…it won't stand when things come to be turned inside out and put down for what they are."”.

questions.prompt: What did the boy do to the pony, and how did the pony respond?
facilitatorNotes: Whipped, kicked and knocked him about the head to make him leap a gate too high; the pony at last threw him into a thorn hedge. John says the pony “shewed no vice.” Ask whether the pony behaved badly.
evidence: a gate that was too high for him
The pony behaved well, sir, and shewed no vice

questions.prompt: Why does John refuse to help the boy, and why does he go to the farmer’s house?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks a few scratches will teach him; he suspects the boy may lie, so he wants to tell the truth first. Readers may disagree about leaving the boy in the hedge.
evidence: maybe a little scratching will teach you
that young fellow is a liar as well as a cruel one

questions.prompt: What did the schoolmaster mean by “the Devil's own trade mark”?
facilitatorNotes: Cruelty shows who a person belongs to, just as a mark shows who made something; love and kindness are God’s mark. Pulling off flies’ wings is the small cruelty that reveals Bill.
evidence: cruelty was the Devil's own trade mark
kind to man and beast, we might know that was God's mark

questions.prompt: John says religion that does not teach kindness “is all a sham.” What does he mean? Do you have to be religious to agree?
facilitatorNotes: A belief is shown by how you treat others, not by talk. Readers of any background may agree that actions show what people truly value; invite reasons, respecting different beliefs.
evidence: there is no religion without love
it is all a sham

readings.title: Black Beauty: James Howard (Chapter XIV)
readings.challenge: Work out what the master is really asking before he explains himself.
readings.focus: The master tests John’s opinion of James, and a new job opens for the young groom.
readings.context: Recap: John told a farmer how his son had beaten a pony, and James remembered how a schoolmaster taught that cruelty is the Devil’s trade mark. A groom looks after horses; a character here means a reference about a worker; livery is a servant’s uniform; to be pensioned off is to retire with an allowance; omnibuses were horse-drawn buses.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, “James Howard,” the whole chapter; opens “One morning early in December, John had just led me into my box after my daily exercise,…”; closes “…people to run into each other, if they did not look sharp and keep their wits about them.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the master ask John so many questions about James? How did you feel reading them?
facilitatorNotes: He wants John’s honest opinion, so he makes it sound as if someone has complained: “if I beat the bush on this side, the birds would fly out.” Readers may have worried for James at first.
evidence: I want to know if you have any complaint to make of James
if I beat the bush on this side, the birds would fly out

questions.prompt: What does John say in James’s defence? What does it show about John?
facilitatorNotes: He refuses to believe gossip without proof and praises James highly, ending “let them come to John Manly.” He is loyal, fair and willing to speak up.
evidence: I don't mean to believe it unless I have it fairly proved before witnesses
let them come to John Manly

questions.prompt: What is good about the job at Clifford Hall, and what does John lose if James takes it?
facilitatorNotes: Wages, clothes, a room and the chance to become coachman one day; John loses “his right hand,” yet would not “stand in his light.” Ask what that phrase means.
evidence: John would lose his right hand
I would not stand in his light for the world

questions.prompt: Why does the master suddenly go to the station and to busy streets so often?
facilitatorNotes: To give James practice in driving among traffic before he leaves. The narrator notices without being told, which makes it gently funny.
evidence: Then it was wonderful what a number of places the master would go to
that bridge wanted good horses and good drivers when the railway bell was ringing

readings.title: Black Beauty: The Old Ostler (Chapter XV)
readings.challenge: Listen for a character’s way of speaking and what it shows about his life.
readings.focus: On the road, a crippled former jockey says he can read a horse’s whole past in twenty minutes.
readings.context: Recap: James is to leave for a better job, and the master has him drive often for practice. An ostler looks after horses at an inn; a drag is a brake on a carriage wheel; a jockey rides in races; Goodwood is a racecourse; “the good book” is the Bible.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, “The Old Ostler,” the whole chapter; opens “After this, it was decided by my master and mistress to pay a visit to some friends who…”; closes “…Ginger, and had brought our corn, and James and the old man left the stable together.”.

questions.prompt: How does James make the long hills easier for the horses?
facilitatorNotes: The drag downhill, the smoothest part of the road, the wheels set across the road for a breathing on long hills, and kind words. “All these little things help a horse very much.”
evidence: He never forgot to put on the drag as we went downhill
All these little things help a horse very much

questions.prompt: How does the old ostler talk? Find words that show his personality.
facilitatorNotes: He repeats “Bless you!” and “ye see,” laughs at himself and rattles on; he is cheerful and proud of his work. Ask readers to read a line aloud in his voice.
evidence: Practice makes perfect
I couldn't whistle if I crawled over my work

questions.prompt: The ostler says he can tell how a horse has been treated in twenty minutes. How?
facilitatorNotes: Calm, quiet horses had good grooms; fretful, nervous or dangerous ones were treated badly, because “their tempers are mostly made when they are young.” Connect to Ginger.
evidence: Give me the handling of a horse for twenty minutes
their tempers are mostly made when they are young

questions.prompt: What does the ostler say about the hunt in which young Gordon and Rob Roy died?
facilitatorNotes: It was a bad place to leap: a thin fence and a steep bank; “a man's life and a horse's life are worth more than a fox's tail.” Compare Duchess in Chapter II.
evidence: a man's life and a horse's life are worth more than a fox's tail

readings.title: Black Beauty: The Fire! (Chapter XVI)
readings.challenge: Notice which senses the narrator uses when he cannot see, and how calm voices change what happens.
readings.focus: A fire breaks out in an inn stable at night, and James leads the horses through the smoke.
readings.context: Recap of Chapters IX–XV: life at Birtwick Park is kind. Black Beauty saved his master by refusing to cross a broken bridge, the Squire speaks out against cruelty, and James Howard is leaving soon for a better job. On a journey with the master and mistress, James has put Black Beauty and Ginger up for the night at an inn, where a cheerful old ostler (stable worker) praised their care. A loft above the stable stores hay; the tap is an inn’s bar.
readings.contentNote: Two horses left in the burning stable die, and the narrator hears them.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI, “The Fire!,” the whole chapter; opens “Later on in the evening, a traveller's horse was brought in by the second ostler, and…”; closes “…two poor horses that could not be got out, were buried under the burnt rafters and tiles.”.

questions.prompt: How does Black Beauty know something is wrong before he sees the fire?
facilitatorNotes: He wakes “very uncomfortable,” the air is thick, Ginger coughs, and he hears “a soft rushing sort of noise, and a low crackling and snapping.” Ask why the writer lets us hear the fire before we see it.
evidence: I woke up very uncomfortable, though I hardly knew why
a low crackling and snapping

questions.prompt: Why won’t the horses go with the first ostler, but go with James?
facilitatorNotes: The ostler is hurried and “frightened himself,” which frightens them; James is “quiet and cheery,” calls them by name and covers Black Beauty’s eyes. Calm is catching, and so is fear.
evidence: so frightened himself that he frightened me still more
James's voice, quiet and cheery, as it always was

questions.prompt: How does Black Beauty help Ginger without being in the stable?
facilitatorNotes: His shrill whinny from the yard gave her courage to come out. Friendship works even at a distance.
evidence: that whinny was the best thing I could have done for her

questions.prompt: How did the fire start? What rule does Black Beauty think should be everywhere?
facilitatorNotes: Dick Towler went up to the hay loft with a pipe, though told to lay it down, and denied it. John’s rule: never a pipe in the stable. One careless act costs two horses their lives.
evidence: Dick denied taking the pipe with him, but no one believed him
never to allow a pipe in the stable

readings.title: Black Beauty: John Manly’s Talk (Chapter XVII)
readings.challenge: Find the saying that John argues against, and the evidence from his own life that he uses.
readings.focus: As James leaves, John explains why he will gladly train a small boy: someone once did the same for him.
readings.context: Recap: James led Black Beauty and Ginger out of a burning stable. A lodge is a gatehouse; the workhouse was a hard place where very poor people were sent to live and work; three shillings a week was a tiny wage; “the ploughtail” means farm work behind a plough.
readings.contentNote: John’s parents died of fever, and he says a selfish person might as well have been “drowned like a puppy or a kitten.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVII, “John Manly's Talk,” the whole chapter; opens “The rest of our journey was very easy, and a little after sunset we reached the house of…”; closes “…and Joe took a great deal of pains to learn, and John was quite encouraged about him.”.

questions.prompt: Why is James doubtful about Joe Green? What reasons does John give for trying him?
facilitatorNotes: Joe is small and only fourteen and a half. John says he is quick, willing and kind-hearted, wants to come, and the master would like to give him a chance.
evidence: why he's a child!
he is quick, and willing, and kind-hearted too

questions.prompt: What happened to John when he was Joe’s age, and who helped him?
facilitatorNotes: His parents died and left him with his crippled sister Nelly; the mistress found Nelly a room and work; the master took him on; old Norman taught him patiently. His kindness to Joe repays what he was given.
evidence: she must have gone to the workhouse, but for our mistress
he was like a father to me

questions.prompt: What does “take care of number one” mean? How does John argue against it?
facilitatorNotes: Look after yourself first. John asks where he, Nelly and the horses would be if others had thought only of themselves: “roasted to death!” Readers can discuss whether there is any truth in the saying.
evidence: Everybody look after himself, and take care of number one.
Where would Black Beauty and Ginger have been if you had only thought of number one?

questions.prompt: How do James and Merrylegs show their feelings about leaving?
facilitatorNotes: James’s voice is thick and he calls it “a real pinch”; Merrylegs pines and loses his appetite. John says he would think less of James if he did not feel it.
evidence: it is a real pinch, John
he pined after him for several days

readings.title: Black Beauty: Going for the Doctor (Chapter XVIII)
readings.challenge: Feel how sentence rhythm creates speed, and notice how a well-meant mistake causes harm.
readings.focus: Black Beauty gallops through the night to save the mistress, then falls ill through a boy’s ignorance.
readings.context: Recap: James has left for his new place, and little Joe Green, fourteen, is learning to help John. A toll-gate stopped travellers until they paid; a cloth is a horse’s blanket; gruel is thin warm porridge; inflammation of the lungs is a serious illness.
readings.contentNote: The mistress is close to death, and Black Beauty becomes dangerously ill.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVIII, “Going for the Doctor,” the whole chapter; opens “One night, a few days after James had left, I had eaten my hay and was laid down in my…”; closes “…John and I must go at the top of our speed, and that it was for the sake of the mistress.”.

questions.prompt: Find a sentence in the gallop that feels fast. How does the writing make it fast?
facilitatorNotes: “We came through a village, then through a dark wood, then uphill, then downhill”: short parts joined by “then” rush past. Compare with the slow, heavy sentences after he gets home.
evidence: we came through a village, then through a dark wood, then uphill, then downhill

questions.prompt: Why does John tell the doctor “You need not take that”? What does it show?
facilitatorNotes: The doctor brings a whip, and John knows Black Beauty “will go till he drops” without one. John trusts the horse and fears for him.
evidence: You need not take that, sir
Black Beauty will go till he drops

questions.prompt: What did Joe do wrong after the ride? Why did he do it?
facilitatorNotes: He did not put on a warm cloth and gave cold water to a hot, wet horse. He thought he was being kind and did “the very best he knew.” The narrator calls it ignorance, not cruelty.
evidence: he did not put my warm cloth on me; he thought I was so hot I should not like it
I am sure he did the very best he knew

questions.prompt: How does Black Beauty feel about the night ride? Did he know why he was running?
facilitatorNotes: He says he knew “John and I must go at the top of our speed,” for the mistress’s sake, though John thought not. Readers can discuss what a horse could really know, and whether the narrator claims too much.
evidence: at least I knew as much as this
it was for the sake of the mistress

readings.title: Black Beauty: Only Ignorance (Chapter XIX)
readings.challenge: Weigh an argument built from examples, and decide whether you agree with its conclusion.
readings.focus: John argues that not knowing can do as much harm as being wicked.
readings.context: Recap: after galloping to fetch the doctor for the mistress, Black Beauty fell very ill because Joe, not knowing better, left him uncovered and gave him cold water. A draught is a dose of medicine; bleeding a sick animal or person was an old treatment, now known to do harm; a hothouse is a heated greenhouse; cuttings are pieces of plants used to grow new ones. In this first edition, one sentence has its quotation marks in the wrong place: “John's voice almost startled me as he answered” is the narrator speaking, and John’s words begin with “Only ignorance!”
readings.contentNote: John tells of a baby who died from wrong medicine and a child left with lasting harm after a fright, using “idiot,” a word once used for people with intellectual disabilities and now considered insulting. Black Beauty is bled as a treatment.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIX, “Only Ignorance,” the whole chapter; opens “I do not know how long I was ill. Mr. Bond, the horse Doctor, came every day. One day he…”; closes “…much better: but I often thought of John's words when I came to know more of the world.”.

questions.prompt: What does Tom ask John to do, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Say a kind word to Joe, who is broken-hearted, cannot eat or smile, and thinks no one will speak to him if Beauty dies. Tom calls it “only ignorance.”
evidence: the boy is quite broken-hearted
I am glad you see it was only ignorance

questions.prompt: Why is John so upset, even though he knows Joe meant no harm?
facilitatorNotes: “That horse is the pride of my heart”; he is “sore” himself. He admits he may be hard on the boy and offers to give him a good word if Beauty is better.
evidence: that horse is the pride of my heart
I know he meant no harm

questions.prompt: What examples does John give that harm can come from people who “did not mean” it?
facilitatorNotes: A nurse whose syrups killed a baby; a boy who frightened his brother into fits; the young ladies who left the hothouse door open. Each one did not intend harm, yet harm happened.
evidence: I suppose Martha Mulwash did not mean to kill that baby
I am sure the young ladies did not mean it, it was only ignorance!

questions.prompt: Is ignorance really “the worst thing in the world, next to wickedness”? What should someone like Joe do about it?
facilitatorNotes: Readers may agree or think John is too hard; the point is that good intentions do not undo harm, so people who care for others must learn. The narrator often thought of John’s words later.
evidence: it is the worst thing in the world, next to wickedness
I often thought of John's words when I came to know more of the world

readings.title: Black Beauty: Joe Green (Chapter XX)
readings.challenge: Watch a character change, and find the moment the change happens.
readings.focus: Joe stops a carter from flogging his horses and becomes, as John says, an inch taller.
readings.context: Recap: Black Beauty recovered from his illness, and John argued that Joe’s mistake, though “only ignorance,” had done real harm. A brickfield is a place where bricks are made; a carter drives a cart; a magistrate is a local judge (the Squire is one); to give evidence is to tell a court what you saw; a summons orders someone to court.
readings.contentNote: A drunken carter swears at and flogs two exhausted horses.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XX, “Joe Green,” the whole chapter; opens “Joe Green went on very well, he learned quickly, and was so attentive and careful, that…”; closes “…and determination in all that he did—as if he had jumped at once from a boy into a man.”.

questions.prompt: What does Joe try first, and what does he do when that fails?
facilitatorNotes: He tells the carter to stop and offers to help lighten the cart; the man refuses, so Joe gallops to Mr. Clay, the master brickmaker. He uses words first, then goes to someone with authority.
evidence: I'll help you to lighten the cart
we were going at a round gallop towards the house of the master brickmaker

questions.prompt: John says “it is everybody's business to interfere.” What does he mean? Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: When we see cruelty, we should not say “'twas not their business.” Readers may discuss how a young person can act safely: Joe asked an adult with authority rather than fighting the man.
evidence: it is everybody's business to interfere when they see it
Many folks would have ridden by

questions.prompt: How has Joe changed since Chapter XVIII? Find the words that show it.
facilitatorNotes: He was the boy whose ignorance made Beauty ill; now he gives evidence clearly, and has “more purpose and determination.” John says he grew an inch taller.
evidence: he had grown an inch taller in that week
as if he had jumped at once from a boy into a man

questions.prompt: Joe was “angry all over.” Is anger ever useful? How did Joe use his?
facilitatorNotes: His anger made him act quickly but he spoke clearly to Mr. Clay and the magistrate; afterwards he was calm. Readers may distinguish anger that hurts from anger that helps.
evidence: I am angry all over, I can tell you
Joe was quite calm by this time

readings.title: Black Beauty: The Parting (Chapter XXI)
readings.challenge: Notice how characters show feelings they cannot speak, and what the last words mean.
readings.focus: The mistress must go abroad for her health, and the Birtwick household breaks up.
readings.context: Recap: Joe Green stopped a carter flogging his horses and gave evidence before the Squire, who is a magistrate. Birtwick has been Black Beauty’s happy home for three years. An earl is a nobleman; an establishment here means a large household with servants and horses; a governess teaches children at home. This is the end of the book’s first part; Black Beauty’s life is about to change.
readings.contentNote: The mistress is seriously ill. Merrylegs is to be shot and buried when he is too old to work, which was then thought the kind way to treat an old horse instead of selling him.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXI, “The Parting,” the whole chapter; opens “I had now lived in this happy place three years, but sad changes were about to come over…”; closes “…the reins, mounted the box, and with Joe drove slowly home; but it was not our home now.”.

questions.prompt: How does the news of the mistress’s illness affect the household? Find a comparison the narrator uses.
facilitatorNotes: It fell “like the tolling of a death-bell”; John is silent and Joe scarcely whistles. Recall the bell in Chapter II.
evidence: like the tolling of a death-bell
John went about his work silent and sad, and Joe scarcely whistled

questions.prompt: What arrangements does the master make for the horses? Why the condition about Merrylegs?
facilitatorNotes: Ginger and Beauty go to the Earl; Merrylegs to the Vicar on condition he is never sold, so he cannot fall into bad hands. Recall Merrylegs’s fear in Chapter IX.
evidence: it was on the condition, that he should never be sold

questions.prompt: What does John decide to do next, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Find work with a colt-breaker, because young horses are spoiled by wrong treatment; he wants to give them “a fair start,” like the title of Chapter V. His choice comes from the book’s lessons.
evidence: Many young animals are frightened and spoiled by wrong treatment
if I could help some of them to a fair start

questions.prompt: How do the characters show feelings at the station without saying them? What does the last line mean?
facilitatorNotes: John makes no answer, the rein twitches, Joe hides his tears by the horses; the train leaves “some very heavy hearts.” “It was not our home now” ends an era and prepares for change.
evidence: perhaps he could not speak
but it was not our home now

readings.title: Black Beauty: Earlshall (Chapter XXII)
readings.challenge: Follow a change that happens “hole by hole,” and notice who is responsible for each step.
readings.focus: At a grand new home the horses must wear the bearing rein for a lady’s sense of style, and Black Beauty learns what it costs.
readings.context: Recap of Chapters I–XXI: Black Beauty, a black horse telling his own life story, was gently raised and trained and spent three happy years at Birtwick Park with kind Squire Gordon, the coachman John Manly and the stable boy Joe Green, beside Ginger, a chestnut mare made fierce by cruel treatment, and Merrylegs the pony. When the mistress fell ill and the family had to go abroad, Ginger and Black Beauty were sold to the Earl of W———, a friend of the Squire. A bearing rein is a strap that holds a carriage horse’s head high; fashionable people liked the proud look, and Sewell wrote this book partly to persuade them to give it up. A gag-bit is a harsh bit used with it. A chaise is a light carriage; boxes are stalls; livery is servants’ uniform; drab is dull brown; imperious means proud and commanding; “by degrees” means a little at a time.
readings.contentNote: The bearing rein causes the horses constant discomfort and pain, and the chapter shows it tightened day by day.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXII, “Earlshall,” the whole chapter; opens “The next morning after breakfast, Joe put Merrylegs into the mistress's low chaise to…”; closes “…though it was now a constant harass instead of a pleasure; but the worst was not come.”.

questions.prompt: What does John Manly tell York about each horse? Why might he leave the bearing rein until last?
facilitatorNotes: The black horse has “the most perfect temper,” never having known a blow; the chestnut was badly treated before, is now willing, but is more easily upset and might “give tit for tat” if ill-used. Only as he is leaving does he mention that neither has worn a bearing rein, and that a dealer blamed the gag-bit for Ginger’s temper. It may be what worries him most, or something he hesitated to raise with the new coachman.
evidence: if she were illused or unfairly treated she would not be unlikely to give tit for tat
the dealer said it was the gag-bit that spoiled the other's temper

questions.prompt: York says he prefers a loose rein, and the Earl says to put it on “easy.” Then who insists on it, and why?
facilitatorNotes: My lady: “she will have style,” and she will not look at carriage horses that are not reined up tight. Two days later she calls them “not fit to be seen.” It is fashion, not need. York and the Earl both give way. Readers can discuss who is responsible: the person who orders a harm, or the people who carry it out.
evidence: but my lady—that's another thing, she will have style
York, you must put those horses' heads higher, they are not fit to be seen.

questions.prompt: How does Black Beauty describe pulling up the steep hill with his head held high? Why is a hill worse?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to put his head forward and “take the carriage up with a will,” but must pull with his head up, which takes “all the spirit out of me” and puts the strain on his back and legs. A horse leans its head and neck into a hard pull; the rein takes that away just when he needs it.
evidence: I had to pull with my head up now, and that took all the spirit out of me
the strain came on my back and legs

questions.prompt: “Day by day, hole by hole.” Why might Sewell show the change so gradually? What does Ginger promise, and what does the last sentence warn?
facilitatorNotes: Each small tightening seems too little to object to, yet “every little makes a difference”; by the end he dreads the harness he used to enjoy. Ginger will say nothing if it gets no worse, but if they strain her tight, “let ’em look out!” The last words, “the worst was not come,” promise trouble. Readers can think of other harms that grow by small steps.
evidence: every little makes a difference, be it for better or worse
but the worst was not come

readings.title: Black Beauty: A Strike for Liberty (Chapter XXIII)
readings.challenge: Weigh how much of the blame for one bad afternoon belongs to each person involved.
readings.focus: Ginger rebels against the tightened rein; Black Beauty, who does not, suffers it for four months with no friend to help him.
readings.context: Recap: at Earlshall, the Earl’s grand house, the coachman York has been tightening Black Beauty’s and Ginger’s bearing reins hole by hole, because the Countess wants her carriage horses’ heads held high for style. Ginger has warned that she will not bear it tight. A strike is a refusal to work, as when workers stop to win better conditions; liberty is freedom. A terret is a ring on the harness that the rein passes through; the carriage pole runs between the two horses; a winch is a crank; a trace is a strap the horse pulls by; the near quarter is the left hindquarter; a hock is the joint halfway up a horse’s hind leg; a hunter is a horse ridden in hunting.
readings.contentNote: Ginger rears, kicks and falls and is bruised; York sits on her head to hold her down; Black Beauty is kicked. The pain of a tight bearing rein is described closely. York grumbles that “if a woman’s husband can’t rule her … a servant can’t,” a period view of wives.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIII, “A Strike for Liberty,” the whole chapter; opens “One day my lady came down later than usual, and the silk rustled more than ever.”; closes “…a matter of course that could not be helped; at any rate nothing was done to relieve me.”.

questions.prompt: What makes Ginger rebel at that exact moment, and what does she do?
facilitatorNotes: The lady orders the heads raised “at once.” York tightens Black Beauty’s rein first; Ginger knows what is coming, and the moment York unhooks her rein to shorten it, she rears, hits his nose, knocks off his hat, and plunges and kicks until she falls over the carriage pole. She chooses her moment: “she took her opportunity.”
evidence: She had a good idea of what was coming
she took her opportunity, and reared up so suddenly

questions.prompt: The chapter is called “A Strike for Liberty.” Did Ginger win?
facilitatorNotes: She is never put in the carriage again, so she escapes the rein, but she is badly bruised and passed to a young son who wants a hunter. Black Beauty, who did not rebel, stays in the carriage with a new partner. Some readers will say she won; others that rebelling cost her too much. The title sounds half admiring, half rueful.
evidence: Ginger was never put into the carriage again
As for me, I was obliged still to go in the carriage

questions.prompt: Who is to blame: my lady, York or Lord W———? What does Black Beauty think?
facilitatorNotes: The lady gave the order; York knew mischief was coming and gave way; the Earl blamed York, but “nothing came of it.” Black Beauty says York “might have stood up better for his horses, but perhaps I am no judge,” a gentle way of judging after all. York’s private grumble blames the husband for not ruling his wife, which readers may find unfair in its own way.
evidence: I thought York might have stood up better for his horses, but perhaps I am no judge.
he blamed York for giving way to his mistress

questions.prompt: What did the dealer tell Max, and what does Black Beauty say about foaming at the mouth? How do these passages work as an argument?
facilitatorNotes: The dealer admits the high rein is “very bad for the horses, but then it is good for trade,” since worn-out horses mean new sales. People admire foam as a sign of spirit, but it is “a sure sign of something wrong.” Sewell argues with a witness, a confession and the horse’s own body, aimed at readers who owned carriages. Ask readers which point is most persuasive, and why.
evidence: of course it is very bad for the horses, but then it is good for trade
It is a sure sign of something wrong, and generally proceeds from suffering.

readings.title: Black Beauty: Lady Anne’s choice of horse (Chapter XXIV, first part)
readings.challenge: Notice the warnings in a conversation, and predict the trouble before it starts.
readings.focus: Lady Anne insists on riding the nervous mare her cousin warns her against, and a sudden fright sends Lizzie off at a gallop.
readings.context: Recap of Chapters XXII–XXIII: Black Beauty and Ginger were sold to the Earl of W——— at Earlshall, where the Countess made them wear a tight bearing rein to hold their heads high for fashion. Ginger rebelled and was taken out of the carriage; Black Beauty bore it for four months. Now it is spring, and the family and the coachman York have gone to London. A side-saddle lets a rider in a long skirt sit with both legs on one side; a habit is a riding dress; a bay is a reddish-brown horse; thoroughbred means of racing stock; amiable means good-natured; to follow the hounds is to hunt on horseback; the curb is part of the bridle that controls the bit; to alight is to get down; frolicsome means playful.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIV, “The Lady Anne, or a Runaway Horse,” from the start through Blantyre setting off after the runaway; opens “Early in the spring, Lord W——— and part of his family went up to London, and took York…”; closes “…he saw it, and giving me a free rein, and leaning a little forward, we dashed after them.”.

questions.prompt: What do we learn about Lady Anne and about Lizzie before the ride?
facilitatorNotes: Lady Anne is “a perfect horse-woman,” gay and gentle, who chose Black Beauty and named him “Black Auster.” Lizzie is a lively, almost thoroughbred bay, a favourite of the gentlemen for her fine action, but Ginger, who knows her, says she is “rather nervous.” The reader is warned before Lady Anne is.
evidence: She was a perfect horse-woman, and as gay and gentle as she was beautiful.
told me she was rather nervous

questions.prompt: Blantyre warns her twice. Why doesn’t she listen? Is she foolish or reasonable?
facilitatorNotes: She has ridden since she was a baby and hunted many times, and she teases him for his “good careful head” and for disapproving of ladies hunting; she may be tired of being told what ladies can do. Her skill is real; the danger is the horse, not the rider. Readers can side with either: she has reason to be confident, but she brushes aside a warning from someone who knows Lizzie.
evidence: pray do not trouble your good careful head about me
she is too nervous for a lady

questions.prompt: What sets Lizzie off? Why might Black Beauty refuse to say which cause it was?
facilitatorNotes: A frisky colt blunders against her hind legs while a boy cracks a great whip. “Whether it was the stupid colt, or the loud cracking of the whip, or both together, I cannot say”: he reports only what he can know. Lady Anne is sitting easily with a loose rein, humming, so the bolt takes her by surprise.
evidence: whether it was the stupid colt, or the loud cracking of the whip, or both together, I cannot say
My young mistress was sitting easily with a loose rein, humming a little song.

questions.prompt: Black Beauty is tied to a gate. What does he do, and what does “I needed no whip, or spur” show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He neighs “again and again” for help, paws the ground and tosses his head to free the rein; when Blantyre mounts, the horse is “as eager as my rider.” He acts as a partner who understands the danger, not a tool. Notice too that Blantyre gives him “a free rein,” the opposite of the carriage.
evidence: I gave a loud shrill neigh for help
I needed no whip, or spur, for I was as eager as my rider

readings.title: Black Beauty: the chase across the common (Chapter XXIV, end)
readings.challenge: Follow a chase through directions shouted by strangers, then hear the ending told second-hand.
readings.focus: Black Beauty and Blantyre race after the runaway; ordinary country people help, and the horse is praised for understanding the danger.
readings.context: Recap: Lady Anne insisted on riding Lizzie, a nervous mare, while her cousin Blantyre rode Black Beauty. Outside the doctor’s house a colt and a cracking whip startled Lizzie into a wild gallop, and Blantyre leapt onto Black Beauty and went after them. A common is open land anyone may use; furze is gorse, a prickly bush; mole turns are molehills; a dyke here is a ditch; clods are lumps of earth; turf-cutters dig up squares of turf to burn; “bean’t” is country speech for “am not”; “afore” means before; Lord George is the Earl’s younger son, and a random rider is a careless one.
readings.contentNote: Lady Anne is thrown and lies pale and unconscious for a long time; she recovers.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIV, “The Lady Anne, or a Runaway Horse,” from the chase along the road to the end of the chapter; opens “For about a mile and a half, the road ran straight, and then bent to the right, after…”; closes “…be able to ride again. This was good news to me, and I looked forward to a happy life.”.

questions.prompt: How do Blantyre and Black Beauty find the way? Who helps them?
facilitatorNotes: A woman at her garden gate points to the right; an old road-mender drops his shovel and calls, “To the common.” Strangers help at once, without stopping the chase. Sewell shows a whole countryside willing to help.
evidence: cried the woman, pointing with her hand
To the common, to the common, sir

questions.prompt: Why is the common “the worst place I ever knew for a headlong gallop”? How does Blantyre ride across it?
facilitatorNotes: It is rough with heather, furze, thorn trees, anthills and molehills. Blantyre guides “with a light hand and a practised eye,” so Black Beauty keeps his pace and clears the ditch and bank in one leap, where Lizzie stumbles and falls. Compare the light hand with the tight bearing rein of the last chapters.
evidence: the worst place I ever knew for a headlong gallop
with a light hand and a practised eye

questions.prompt: What does the turf-cutter say when Blantyre asks if he can ride? Why is his answer moving?
facilitatorNotes: He is no horseman, but he would “risk my neck for the Lady Anne” because she was kind to his wife in the winter. A poor working man repays a lady’s kindness; he rides “manfully,” refuses a drink, and hurries back. Black Beauty calls him “a good man and true.”
evidence: I'd risk my neck for the Lady Anne; she was uncommon good to my wife in the winter.
he did his errand like a good man and true

questions.prompt: Black Beauty does not see Lady Anne rescued; Ginger tells him. Why might Sewell tell it this way? What worry is tucked into the end of the chapter?
facilitatorNotes: A horse can tell only what a horse saw or heard, and Ginger’s short, uncertain report (“she is not dead”) keeps the suspense. Then, among the good news and Blantyre’s praise, Ginger comes back from hunting with Lord George strained and coughing, with “too much spirit to complain.” Black Beauty hopes for “a happy life,” but readers may sense trouble ahead.
evidence: all that I heard was, 'she is not dead.'
She had too much spirit to complain, but I could not help feeling anxious about her.

readings.title: Black Beauty: Reuben Smith (Chapter XXV)
readings.challenge: Read the signs of trouble the narrator notices before he names their cause.
readings.focus: A skilled and likeable groom’s one great fault, drink, ruins a journey, and Black Beauty pays with his knees.
readings.context: Recap: at Earlshall, Black Beauty helped save Lady Anne when a nervous mare bolted with her, and he was praised for it. The Earl’s family and the coachman York are in London, and the stables are left to Reuben Smith. A farrier shoes and treats horses; a four-in-hand is a carriage drawn by four horses and a tandem by two, one in front of the other; an under situation is a junior job; to intercede is to plead for someone; a brougham is a closed carriage; a prig is a conceited young man; an ostler cares for horses at an inn; a turnpike gate is where travellers paid a toll; the quick is the tender living part inside a hoof.
readings.contentNote: Reuben Smith gets drunk, curses, and whips Black Beauty into a gallop over sharp new stones with a loose shoe; the horse falls, his hoof split and his knees cut, and Smith is thrown and lies groaning, then still. The chapter says drink made him “a terror to his wife.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXV, “Reuben Smith,” the whole chapter; opens “I must now say a little about Reuben Smith, who was left in charge of the stables when…”; closes “…ago, when I used to lie beside my mother in the green pleasant meadow at Farmer Grey's.”.

questions.prompt: What kind of man is Reuben Smith when he is “all right”? Why was he taken back after being dismissed?
facilitatorNotes: He understands horses, is gentle and clever, can doctor them almost like a farrier, drives superbly, and is handsome, educated and pleasant; everyone likes him. York pleaded for him, the Earl is kind-hearted, and Smith promised never to drink again, and kept his promise for a long time. Sewell makes him likeable so that what happens is sadder.
evidence: No one more thoroughly understood his business than he did
the man had promised faithfully that he would never taste another drop

questions.prompt: Before he says “drunk,” what signs does Black Beauty notice that something is wrong?
facilitatorNotes: Smith comes an hour late, having “met with some old friends”; he waves away the loose nail “in a very loud off-hand way,” which is unlike him; he does not come until nearly nine; his voice is loud and rough, he abuses the ostler, and he answers the landlord’s warning with an oath. The horse reads behaviour, and the reader pieces it together before the word appears.
evidence: I thought it very unlike him, not to see about the shoe
He seemed in a very bad temper, and abused the ostler

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for the accident? Think about Smith, York, the Earl and the loose nail.
facilitatorNotes: Smith most of all: “If Smith had been in his right senses” he would have felt the horse go wrong. But York had hushed up his earlier bouts, the Earl gave him another chance, and the loose nail was found late. Readers can discuss whether the second chance was a mistake or a kindness that Smith alone betrayed.
evidence: If Smith had been in his right senses, he would have been sensible of something wrong in my pace
York had hushed the matter up, and kept it from the Earl's knowledge

questions.prompt: Read the last paragraph again. Why does the calm April night make the scene more painful? What does Black Beauty remember, and why then?
facilitatorNotes: A nightingale sings, white clouds drift, an owl flits over the hedge: everything is peaceful around a man lying still and a horse in silent pain, listening for help that may not come for hours. He remembers lying beside his mother at Farmer Grey’s, his first and safest home, perhaps because he longs for comfort, perhaps to show how far he has come from it. Ask readers what they think has happened to Smith.
