evidence: horses are used to bear their pain in silence
when I used to lie beside my mother in the green pleasant meadow at Farmer Grey's

readings.title: Black Beauty: How it Ended (Chapter XXVI)
readings.challenge: Follow how the truth about the accident comes out, first to the men on the road and then at the inquest.
readings.focus: Reuben Smith is found dead, Black Beauty is cleared of blame but scarred for life, and Smith’s widow and children lose their home.
readings.context: Recap: Reuben Smith, the Earl’s groom, got drunk at the White Lion inn and galloped Black Beauty home over sharp new stones although one shoe was loose. The horse fell and Smith was thrown; Chapter XXV ended near midnight with Smith lying still in the road and Black Beauty standing beside him, cut and in pain. A dog-cart is a light two-wheeled cart; a box is a stall where a horse can move about; a bran poultice is a warm wet dressing of bran; proud flesh is swollen flesh that grows in a healing wound; caustic is a burning chemical; a blemish is a scar that spoils a horse’s looks; an inquest is an official inquiry into a sudden death; intoxicated means drunk. The Union House was the workhouse, where people with no money and no home were sent to live and work.
readings.contentNote: Reuben Smith is found dead with his hair soaked in blood; Black Beauty’s wounds are treated painfully; Smith’s widow cries out against “that cursed drink” and is sent with her six children to the workhouse.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXVI, “How it ended,” the whole chapter; opens “It must have been nearly midnight, when I heard at a great distance the sound of a…”; closes “…leave the pleasant home by the tall oak trees, and go into that great gloomy Union House.”.

questions.prompt: How does Black Beauty know that help is coming, long before he can see it?
facilitatorNotes: By sound alone: a horse’s feet far off, fading and returning, then a step he is “almost sure” is Ginger’s, then the sound of the dog-cart. He neighs, and she answers. A horse in the dark knows his friend by her step.
evidence: I was almost sure I could distinguish Ginger's step
I neighed loudly, and was overjoyed to hear an answering neigh from Ginger

questions.prompt: At first the men think the horse threw Reuben. What makes Robert change his mind?
facilitatorNotes: He finds the hoof “cut all to pieces” and no shoe, so the horse fell because he was ridden over the stones unshod. No sober rider would have done that, and Robert guesses it was “the old thing over again,” drink. The inquest later agrees, and Black Beauty is cleared.
evidence: his hoof is cut all to pieces
I'm afraid it has been the old thing over again
I was cleared of all blame

questions.prompt: Ginger stands “as still as a stone” while the body is lifted into the cart. Why does Black Beauty mention it?
facilitatorNotes: Her usual fault is impatience in standing, so her stillness is unusual. He believes she understood what was happening and stood still out of something like respect. Sewell wants readers to see that horses notice and feel more than people think; some readers may say Ginger was simply tired or frightened.
evidence: she knew as well as I did, what was going on, and stood as still as a stone
if she had a fault, it was that she was impatient in standing

questions.prompt: Whom does Susan blame for Reuben’s death? Do you agree, and why might Sewell end the chapter with her and her children?
facilitatorNotes: She blames the drink and those who sell it, and insists Reuben “was so good.” Readers may answer that Reuben chose to drink, or that the inn served him knowing his weakness, or both. The chapter ends with a widow and six children sent to the “great gloomy Union House”: the people who did nothing wrong pay most. Some readers will think Susan too forgiving; others that grief makes her loyal.
evidence: it was all that cursed drink; why will they sell that cursed drink?
go into that great gloomy Union House

readings.title: Black Beauty: Ruined, and Going Down-hill (Chapter XXVII)
readings.challenge: Notice what the chapter title promises, and look for the signs that Black Beauty’s life is changing for the worse.
readings.focus: Black Beauty and Ginger, both injured through other people’s carelessness, spend a last summer together before he is sold away.
readings.context: Recap of Chapters XXII–XXVI: Black Beauty and his friend Ginger were sold to the Earl of W——— at Earlshall. The Earl’s son, Lord George, took Ginger as his hunting horse. One night the groom Reuben Smith, drunk, galloped Black Beauty over sharp stones with a loose shoe; the horse fell and Smith was killed. The inquest cleared Black Beauty, but his knees are scarred for life. A steeple chase is a race across country over hedges and ditches; a horse’s “wind” is its breathing, and “touched” means damaged; a twelve-month’s run is a year out at grass; livery stables keep horses and carriages to hire out; a horse box is a railway wagon for horses; a chaise is a light carriage. Three hundred pounds, the price of the pair, was a great deal of money. Bath is a city in the west of England.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXVII, “Ruined, and going Down-hill,” the whole chapter; opens “As soon as my knees were sufficiently healed, I was turned into a small meadow for a…”; closes “…at others, the horse and chaise were let to gentlemen or ladies who drove themselves.”.

questions.prompt: What happened to Ginger after Black Beauty left the stable?
facilitatorNotes: Lord George rode her in a steeple chase though the groom warned she was strained. She came in with the first three, but her breathing was damaged and her back strained, so she was “turned off” to the meadow to see whether rest would cure her.
evidence: though the groom told him she was a little strained, and was not fit for the race
she had been ruined by hard riding, and was now turned off to see what rest would do

questions.prompt: Ginger says they were ruined “you by a drunkard, and I by a fool.” Are those fair names for Reuben Smith and Lord George?
facilitatorNotes: Both men ignored a warning and a horse paid for it. “Fool” fits a young man who “would take no warning.” Some readers will think “drunkard” too harsh for a man everyone liked; others that “fool” is too gentle for someone who knew his horse was strained and rode her anyway.
evidence: Lord George was young and would take no warning
ruined in the prime of our youth and strength—you by a drunkard, and I by a fool

questions.prompt: What does the Earl care about most, and what does he decide? What does that show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He minds the wasted money, but cares most that his old friend’s horses are ruined. Ginger gets a year’s rest; the black horse must be sold, because scarred knees will not do in a grand stable. He asks York to choose the new place with care. He is kind, but looks still decide Black Beauty’s fate; readers may weigh which matters more.
evidence: what I care most for is, that these horses of my old friend
I could not have knees like these in my stables
I should be more particular about the place than the money he would fetch

questions.prompt: How does the chapter show that Black Beauty is “going Down-hill”? Is his new home really worse?
facilitatorNotes: He loses Ginger without a goodbye, travels by noisy train, and stands in a stall on a slope with his head tied: less comfortable and less free than before. Yet he is well fed and cleaned, and the master takes “as much care of us as he could.” The fall is gradual: each home a little lower. Readers may argue the change is small so far, and predict what comes next.
evidence: she trotted anxiously along by the hedge, calling to me as long as she could hear the sound of my feet
The stalls were laid on a slope instead of being level

readings.title: Black Beauty: A Job Horse and his Drivers (Chapter XXVIII)
readings.challenge: Sort the kinds of bad driving Black Beauty describes, and compare two men’s reactions to the same lame horse.
readings.focus: Hired out to anyone who pays, Black Beauty meets tight-rein and loose-rein drivers, and one careless driver lames him with a stone in his hoof.
readings.context: Recap: with his knees scarred, Black Beauty was sold to the master of livery stables in Bath, who hires out horses and carriages. A job-horse is one hired out by the day or the job to anyone who pays. The reins run from the driver’s hands to the bit in the horse’s mouth, so every pull is felt there. A phaeton is a light open carriage; the frog is the soft V-shaped part on the underside of a hoof; a cob is a short, sturdy horse; the near foot is the left one; “playing the old soldier” means pretending to be ill to get out of work; “here’s a go” means “what a fix”; a stone-pick is a hooked tool for getting stones out of hooves.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXVIII, “A Job Horse and his Drivers,” the whole chapter; opens “Hitherto I had always been driven by people who at least knew how to drive; but in this…”; closes “This was the sort of experience we job-horses often came in for.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Black Beauty think he was hired out to ignorant drivers more often than other horses?
facilitatorNotes: Because he was good-tempered and gentle and “could be depended upon.” His good nature is exactly what exposes him to the worst drivers, which is unfair.
evidence: as I was good-tempered and gentle, I think I was oftener let out to the ignorant drivers

questions.prompt: What is wrong with tight-rein drivers, and what is wrong with loose-rein drivers? What would a good driver do instead?
facilitatorNotes: Tight-rein drivers pull on the mouth all the time, as if the horse could not hold himself up, which torments a horse with a tender mouth. Loose-rein drivers have no control when something happens suddenly and let a horse slip into lazy habits. A good driver keeps a light feel of the rein and keeps the horse to its best paces and manners, as Squire Gordon did.
evidence: just as if a horse was not made to hold himself up
one likes to feel the rein a little in going down-hill

questions.prompt: When Black Beauty goes lame, what does the driver say, and what does the farmer do? What does each notice?
facilitatorNotes: The driver notices nothing for half a mile, then blames the stables and accuses the horse of shamming. The farmer sees the trouble at a glance, gets down, removes the stone with care, and advises gentle driving. One looks at the horse; the other looks at the scenery and his passengers.
evidence: Why they have sent us out with a lame horse! What a shame!
he goes very much as if he had a stone in his shoe

questions.prompt: “I never knew that horses picked up stones before.” Is the driver cruel, or only ignorant? Does the difference matter to the horse?
facilitatorNotes: He is not deliberately cruel; he did not know. But the horse suffered as much, and even afterwards the man flops the reins and whips the harness. Black Beauty cannot tell whether he was “partly blind, or only very careless.” Some readers will say ignorance is easier to forgive; others that anyone who hires a horse ought to learn how to care for one.
evidence: that is a queer thing! I never knew that horses picked up stones before.
Whether the man was partly blind, or only very careless, I can't say

readings.title: Black Beauty: Cockneys (Chapter XXIX, first part)
readings.challenge: Hear when Black Beauty is mimicking other people’s thoughts, and decide who is to blame for an accident on a blind corner.
readings.focus: Townspeople who drive a hired horse like a machine wear him out, and one reckless driver wrecks Black Beauty’s partner, Rory.
readings.context: Recap: Black Beauty, now a job-horse hired out from livery stables in Bath, has been describing the bad drivers he meets: tight-rein drivers who never ease the bit, and careless loose-rein drivers, one of whom drove him half a mile with a sharp stone wedged in his hoof. A Cockney is strictly a Londoner; here, scornfully, any townsman who knows nothing of horses. The drag, or drag-shoe, is an iron shoe slipped under a wheel to slow a carriage going downhill; to be thrown “on our haunches” is to be jerked back onto the hindquarters; a gig is a light two-wheeled carriage pulled between two shafts; a pair of horses pulls on either side of a single pole; coal carting is pulling heavy carts of coal.
readings.contentNote: A carriage shaft is driven into a horse’s chest; he is torn open and bleeding, and the narrator says it would have been better for him to have been killed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIX, “Cockneys,” from the start through Rory’s accident; opens “Then there is the steam-engine style of driving; these drivers were mostly people from…”; closes “…cart behind him, on which no drag could be placed, make me sad even now to think of.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Black Beauty call it the “steam-engine style of driving”?
facilitatorNotes: These drivers come from towns and travel by rail, so they treat a horse like a small engine: they have paid, so it must go at the same pace, however heavy the load or steep the road, with no rest. A machine does not tire; a horse does.
evidence: They always seemed to think that a horse was something like a steam-engine, only smaller.

questions.prompt: “Oh, no, they have paid to ride, and ride they will!” Whose voice is this? How does it change at the end of the paragraph?
facilitatorNotes: Black Beauty is mimicking the drivers’ thoughts, with their exclamations, scornfully, as if quoting them. At the end he returns to his own voice for the horses, “uncomplaining and obedient.” The mockery shows how angry Sewell is. Some readers will take it as words the drivers really said aloud.
evidence: Oh, no, they have paid to ride, and ride they will! The horse? Oh, he's used to it!
uncomplaining and obedient, though often sorely harassed and down-hearted

questions.prompt: What caused Rory’s accident, and who was to blame?
facilitatorNotes: The other driver came fast down the hill and cut the blind corner on the wrong side, so he could not pull over in time. Black Beauty’s own driver kept to his side near the hedge. Black Beauty blames drivers who do not know or care which side is theirs. Some readers may say his own driver should also have slowed at a corner he could not see round.
evidence: The man who was driving, was making straight for the corner
who don't even know which is their own side of the road, or if they know, don't care

questions.prompt: Why does Black Beauty say it would have been “a good thing” if the wound had killed Rory?
facilitatorNotes: Because once injured Rory was worth less, and was sold for coal carting, hauling heavy loads up and down steep hills, work so hard that “only horses know” what it is. Black Beauty, scarred himself, knows a damaged horse sinks to harder work. Many readers will find this shocking; ask whether they agree that some lives are worse than death, or think he is wrong.
evidence: and a good thing for him, poor fellow, if it had
he was sold for coal carting; and what that is, up and down those steep hills, only horses know

readings.title: Black Beauty: Peggy, a shying horse and a good driver (Chapter XXIX, end)
readings.challenge: Listen to two horses explain their “bad habits,” and look for what the habits have in common.
readings.focus: A short-legged mare and a nervous young horse tell how whipping made their faults, and a gentleman who checks the harness wins Black Beauty’s trust.
readings.context: Recap: Black Beauty, a job-horse at livery stables in Bath, has been describing “Cockneys,” drivers who treat a horse like a steam-engine. One of them crashed into Rory, his partner in a pair, who was badly hurt and sold for coal carting. Dun is a dull yellowish brown; dappled means marked with round spots; a canter is a pace faster than a trot; desponding means hopeless; a capital master is an excellent one; blinkers are leather flaps beside a horse’s eyes so that he sees only forward; to shy is to jump aside in fright; a shindy is a fuss; a curb is a bit with a chain under the jaw that can hurt when pulled; “put the rein in at the cheek” means fasten it so that the curb does not act. Pultney Street is a grand street in Bath.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXIX, “Cockneys,” from Peggy’s story to the end of the chapter; opens “After Rory was disabled, I often went in the carriage with a mare named Peggy, who stood…”; closes “…horse for riding. And so it came to pass that in the summer I was sold to Mr. Barry.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Peggy go with such an odd pace?
facilitatorNotes: Her legs are short, so she cannot keep up with longer-legged horses, and drivers in a hurry whipped her for it. She learned to give a little spring forward to keep up. With her first master, a country clergyman who was never in a hurry, she trotted steadily.
evidence: it is just because my legs are so short
so I got into this way of making a spring forward to keep up

questions.prompt: Peggy and the young horse who shies both explain a habit people blame them for. What do their stories have in common?
facilitatorNotes: In both, whipping made the habit or made it worse: Peggy was whipped for being slow, the young horse for being frightened, which frightened him more. Both habits come from what people did, not from bad nature. The old gentleman’s advice says it exactly.
evidence: he shys because he is frightened, and you only frighten him more
all the whipping comes to their share, and they can't help it

questions.prompt: What does the tall gentleman do before he drives off, and what does Black Beauty learn from it?
facilitatorNotes: He checks the bit and bridle, shifts the collar to see that it fits, asks whether a curb is needed and has it taken off, and drives with a light rein. Black Beauty knows at once that someone behind him “knew how a good horse ought to be driven,” and it feels “like old times again.”
evidence: he looked at the bit and bridle, and just shifted the collar with his hand, to see if it fitted comfortably
with a light feel of the rein

questions.prompt: Rory, Peggy and Black Beauty all leave these stables. What decides whether each one ends up well or badly?
facilitatorNotes: Rory, wrecked by a careless driver, goes to coal carting; Peggy is sold to two gentle ladies; Black Beauty is bought for Mr. Barry because a gentleman liked him. Mostly it is luck: who drives them and who buys them, not their own goodness. Black Beauty says Peggy “deserved a good place,” but Rory deserved one too. Some readers will argue Black Beauty earned his luck with his good mouth and willing pace.
evidence: she deserved a good place
This gentleman took a great liking to me

readings.title: Black Beauty: A Thief! (Chapter XXX)
readings.challenge: Notice what Black Beauty knows that his master does not, and how the truth finally comes out.
readings.focus: A groom secretly steals Black Beauty’s oats until a sharp-eyed farmer notices the horse growing weak.
readings.context: Recap of Chapters XXVI–XXIX: after a drunken groom’s fall left his knees scarred, Black Beauty was sold to livery stables in Bath and hired out to all sorts of drivers, good and bad. A gentleman who drove him well persuaded the owner to sell him to a friend, Mr. Barry, who wanted a safe horse to ride. Corn here means oats; crushed beans, bran (the husks of grain), vetches and rye grass are horse foods; an ostler looks after horses at an inn; Wells is a small cathedral city near Bath; “fiddlestick!” means “nonsense!”; to stint is to give too little; “shew” is an old spelling of “show”; a lock-up is a small jail. “Dumb” here means unable to speak.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXX, “A Thief!”, the whole chapter; opens “My new master was an unmarried man. He lived at Bath, and was much engaged in business.…”; closes “…the boy was not held to be guilty, but the man was sentenced to prison for two months.”.

questions.prompt: The new groom is called Filcher; “to filch” means to steal small things. What does the name tell you, and does he seem a thief at first?
facilitatorNotes: The name warns the reader before anything happens. But at first he seems a good groom: he keeps the stable clean and airy, grooms thoroughly, and is gentle. Sewell lets the reader suspect while the horse and the master do not.
evidence: engaged a man named Filcher as groom
He kept the stable clean and airy, and he groomed me thoroughly

questions.prompt: What excuse does the groom give for the horse’s dullness, and how does the farmer see through it?
facilitatorNotes: Filcher says horses are always dull and weak in autumn. The farmer points out it is only August, and feels that the horse is warm and damp after gentle riding, like a horse fed on grass, not oats. He reads the horse’s body instead of trusting the groom.
evidence: why this is only August
he is as warm and damp as a horse just come up from grass

questions.prompt: “Dumb beasts!” yes, we are. Why does this matter so much in the chapter, and in the whole book?
facilitatorNotes: Black Beauty saw the boy fill a bag with oats every morning and could have told his master, but a horse cannot speak, so the theft went on for two months. The whole book imagines what a horse would say if he could; Sewell wrote it to speak for animals who cannot speak for themselves.
evidence: but if I could have spoken, I could have told my master where his oats went to

questions.prompt: The boy was “not held to be guilty,” but his father went to prison. Was that fair to the boy? Who else, if anyone, shares the blame?
facilitatorNotes: The boy was doing what his father told him, and he was frightened and cried; most readers will agree he should not be punished like a man. Some may say he must have known it was wrong. Mr. Barry “knew very little about horses” and did not notice for two months, though the farmer does not blame him.
evidence: the boy was not held to be guilty, but the man was sentenced to prison for two months
My master knew very little about horses

readings.title: Black Beauty: A Humbug! (Chapter XXXI)
readings.challenge: Compare what the new groom does when his master is watching with what he does when nobody is.
readings.focus: A vain, flattering groom makes Black Beauty look smart and leaves him standing in filth until his feet go bad.
readings.context: Recap: Black Beauty’s master, Mr. Barry, a businessman in Bath who knows little about horses, bought him for riding. His first groom, Filcher, stole the horse’s oats until a farmer friend noticed, and Filcher went to prison. A humbug is a fraud, a person who pretends; a crupper is a strap under the tail that keeps the saddle in place; a loose box is a stall where a horse can move about; indolent means lazy; vapours are fumes, here from rotting wet straw; fumble-footed means clumsy; green meat is fresh grass; a bran mash is a warm soft feed; horse balls and draughts are medicine pills and drinks; thrush is an infection of the hoof caused by standing in wet, dirty bedding; Lansdown is a hill above Bath; tow is coarse fibre; liniment is medicine rubbed on.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXXI, “A Humbug!”, the whole chapter; opens “My master was not immediately suited, but in a few days my new groom came. He was a tall,…”; closes “…wanted one. I was therefore kept till my feet were quite sound, and was then sold again.”.

questions.prompt: What does Alfred Smirk do well, and what does he leave undone? Who is each kind of work for?
facilitatorNotes: He strokes and pats the horse when his master is watching, wets the mane and tail and oils the hoofs to make the horse look smart at the door. He neglects the feet, shoes, grooming, bit, saddle, crupper and the stall. The showy work is for his master’s eyes; the hidden work, which keeps a horse healthy, he skips.
evidence: he did a great deal of stroking and patting, when his master was there to see it
He left my bit rusty, my saddle damp, and my crupper stiff.

questions.prompt: How does Alfred get out of scrubbing the stall? Look closely at what he says.
facilitatorNotes: He agrees politely, with “sir” at every turn, but warns that water might give the horse a cold, so the master backs down; then he agrees the drain might be to blame. The bricklayer finds nothing, charges five shillings, and the smell goes on. Alfred never says no; he steers his master away from the real cause.
evidence: it is rather dangerous, sir, throwing down water in a horse's box
found nothing amiss; so he put down some lime, and charged the master five shillings

questions.prompt: “I have noticed the same myself, when I have exercised him.” Why does Black Beauty correct this at once?
facilitatorNotes: It is a lie: Alfred hardly ever exercised him, and the horse often stood for days without stretching his legs. The master cannot know this; the horse does, and as narrator he can at last tell the reader what he could never tell his master.
evidence: Now the fact was, that he hardly ever did exercise me

questions.prompt: Mr. Barry has been “twice deceived.” Is he partly to blame?
facilitatorNotes: He knew little about horses, trusted appearances and polite manners, and did not look into his stable, though the farmer had warned him to. But he did notice the smell and the stumbling, asked questions and went to a farrier. Some readers will say a busy man cannot be expected to be an expert; others that whoever keeps a horse must learn to care for it. His answer is to stop keeping a horse at all.
evidence: every one thought he was a very nice young man
Mr. Barry was so much disgusted at being twice deceived by his grooms

readings.title: Black Beauty: A Horse Fair (Chapter XXXII)
readings.challenge: See a horse fair through the eyes of a horse for sale, and notice how he judges the people who judge him.
readings.focus: Sold again because of his scarred knees, Black Beauty watches the buyers at a horse fair and is bought by a cheerful London cabman.
readings.context: Black Beauty (1877) is the only book by the English writer Anna Sewell, who wrote it during her last years of illness and died a few months after it was published. A horse tells his own life story, and Sewell meant it to make people kinder to horses, which in her time pulled almost every cart, cab and carriage. Black Beauty has had several owners since a drunken groom’s fall scarred his knees. The scars spoil his looks, though he is still strong and sound, so gentlemen will no longer buy him. Now he is taken to a horse fair to be sold again. Merrylegs was a pony at his first good home; horses with “knees knuckling over” have weak legs that bend forward; unsoundness of wind is damaged breathing; “running up and beating down” is bargaining the price up and down; “a slip in the stall” would mean the knees were hurt in the stable. Twenty-four pounds ten is £24 and ten shillings (twenty shillings made a pound); a sixpence was a small coin; “governor” is a friendly word for a man in charge; cab work is pulling a cab, a horse-drawn taxi; “Done” means “It’s a deal”; a thoroughfare is a main road; a bran mash is a warm soft feed for a horse.
readings.contentNote: Worn-out horses at the fair are painfully thin, lame, and covered in old sores.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXXII, “A Horse Fair,” the whole chapter; opens “No doubt a horse fair is a very amusing place to those who have nothing to lose; at any…”; closes “…of dry straw, and after a capital supper, I laid down, thinking I was going to be happy.”.

questions.prompt: Black Beauty sees three kinds of horses at the fair. What are they, and why are the last ones “sad sights for a horse to look upon”?
facilitatorNotes: Young horses and splendid ones in their prime, showing off; good horses like himself who have fallen “into the middle class” through an accident or blemish; and broken-down old horses at the back, thin and sore, with no hope left. They are sad to him because he may become one of them.
evidence: fallen into the middle class, through some accident or blemish
who knows not but he may come to the same state

questions.prompt: How does Black Beauty judge the buyers? What does he notice about the grey-eyed man?
facilitatorNotes: By the way they handle him: some roughly “as if one was only a piece of wood,” some gently. The grey-eyed man is small and quick, used to horses, speaks gently, has a kindly eye, and smells fresh, “as if he had come out of a hayloft,” not of beer and tobacco. The horse judges by touch, voice and smell.
evidence: Of course I judged a good deal of the buyers by their manners to myself.
a fresh smell as if he had come out of a hayloft

questions.prompt: Follow the bargaining. What does Black Beauty do while it goes on, and what does he call the man before the sale is even settled?
facilitatorNotes: The hard-faced man offers twenty-three pounds; the grey-eyed man comes back and offers twenty-four; the salesman asks twenty-five; he settles at twenty-four pounds ten, firmly. A horse cannot choose his buyer, but Black Beauty reaches out his head toward the man he wants, and already calls him “my friend.”
evidence: I could not help reaching out my head towards him.
said my friend, in a very decided tone

questions.prompt: The chapter ends “thinking I was going to be happy.” What makes him think so, and why might a reader feel a little uneasy?
facilitatorNotes: The cabmen’s cheerful greeting, the whole family running out, Dolly patting him without fear, a bran mash, the boy’s joke and the laughter, a clean stall. But after so many homes the word “thinking” can sound like a warning, and the salesman mentioned “cab work,” which is hard. Ask readers to predict, and keep their guesses for later chapters.
evidence: At once the little hand was patting about all over my shoulder without fear; how good it felt!
I laid down, thinking I was going to be happy

readings.title: Black Beauty: A London Cab Horse (Chapter XXXIII)
readings.challenge: Collect what Jerry Barker does for his horses, and notice how the other cabmen size up a newcomer.
readings.focus: Black Beauty begins work as a London cab horse with a kind master, a happy family and a wise old partner, Captain.
readings.context: Black Beauty (1877) is the only book by the English writer Anna Sewell, who wrote it during her last years of illness and died a few months after it was published. A horse tells his own life story, and Sewell meant it to make people kinder to horses, which in her time pulled almost every cart, cab and carriage. After a drunken groom’s fall scarred his knees, Black Beauty passed through several owners. At a horse fair he was bought by Jeremiah Barker, a London cab driver, who rode him home to his wife Polly and their children Harry and Dolly. A cab was a horse-drawn carriage for hire, like a taxi; cabmen waited in a line, the rank, at a cab stand. The Crimean War (1853–56) was fought by Britain, France and Turkey against Russia; cavalry are soldiers on horseback. “A regular brick” means a thoroughly good sort; a crupper is a strap under the tail; a bearing rein holds a horse’s head painfully high (Black Beauty suffered one at Earlshall); a curb is a bit with a chain under the jaw that can hurt; a snaffle is the simplest, gentlest bit; palisades (printed “pallisades”) are fences of iron rails; a comforter is a woollen scarf. Black horses usually pulled funeral carriages. “Black Beauty” was the name his first good owners gave him.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXXIII, “A London Cab Horse,” the whole chapter; opens “My new master's name was Jeremiah Barker, but as every one called him Jerry, I shall do…”; closes “…company, and chat a bit. It was on these days that I learned my companion's history.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Jerry decide to give the horse “the benefit of the doubt” about his knees? What does the phrase mean?
facilitatorNotes: No one can tell him whose fault the broken knees were, so he will not assume the worst, and judges by what he has seen: “a firmer, neater stepper, I never rode.” Giving the benefit of the doubt means choosing to believe the better explanation when you cannot know. The gentlemen at the fair did the opposite.
evidence: as long as I don't know, I shall give him the benefit of the doubt

questions.prompt: The family names him “Jack,” after their old horse. How do you think Black Beauty feels about his new name?
facilitatorNotes: He does not complain, and is glad of their petting. But he says they treated him as if he were the “Black Beauty” of olden time, which suggests the old name belongs to a past life he still remembers. Readers may think he minds, or that kindness matters more to him than a name; Polly likes “to keep a good name going,” so the name is meant as an honour.
evidence: made as much of me as if I had been the "Black Beauty" of olden time
we'll call him 'Jack,' after the old one

questions.prompt: At the cab stand the men “pass their remarks.” What do they say, and how does Jerry answer?
facilitatorNotes: One says he is good for a funeral; Jones says he is too smart-looking and must have something wrong with him. Jerry answers good-humouredly that he will not look for trouble before it finds him. Then Grey Grant, whom everyone respects, looks him over and says he is “the right sort,” and that settles it.
evidence: I suppose I need not find it out till it finds me out
He's the right sort for you, Jerry

questions.prompt: List what Jerry does for his horses. Which do you think matters most to Black Beauty, and why?
facilitatorNotes: He fits the collar and bridle carefully, uses no bearing rein or curb, hardly uses the whip, fixes bars so they can turn round at night and touch noses, keeps them clean, varies their food, and rests them on Sundays. Black Beauty says Sundays were best; but after Earlshall the plain snaffle (“What a blessing that was!”) may matter as much, and some readers will choose being able to touch Captain’s nose.
evidence: nothing but a plain ring snaffle. What a blessing that was!
But the best thing we had was, our Sundays for rest

readings.title: Black Beauty: Seedy Sam (Chapter XXXIX)
readings.challenge: Follow a working man’s arithmetic, and decide where he says the blame belongs.
readings.focus: A worn-out cab driver tells the other cabmen why he cannot help overworking his horse, and a few days later he is dead.
readings.context: Black Beauty (1877) is the only book by the English writer Anna Sewell, who wrote it during her last years of illness and died a few months after it was published. A horse tells his own life story, and Sewell meant it to make people kinder to horses, which in her time pulled almost every cart, cab and carriage. Black Beauty now pulls a London cab for Jerry Barker, who owns his cab and is kind to his horses. Many cabmen owned nothing: they rented a cab and horses from a cab-owner, here Skinner, for a fixed sum each day and kept only what they earned beyond it, while the law fixed the fares they could charge. The Governor is the oldest driver on the stand, the place where cabs wait in a line (the rank). Twelve pence made a shilling; to pledge a thing is to pawn it for a loan; a macintosh is a raincoat; a dram is a small glass of spirits; to “blow him up” is to scold him; “hard lines” means hard luck. Labor Day honors working people and the fight for shorter hours and days of rest.
readings.contentNote: A man dies of overwork and fever, leaving a poor family. The cabmen speak of whipping tired horses and of drinking.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXXIX, “Seedy Sam,” the whole chapter; opens “I should say, that for a cab-horse I was very well off indeed; my driver was my owner,…”; closes “…awhile, and then the Governor said, "I tell you what, mates, this is a warning for us."”.

questions.prompt: Sam must earn eighteen shillings a day for Skinner before he keeps a penny. Work through his morning as he tells it. How far has his horse gone, how much has he taken, and how far short is he still?
facilitatorNotes: A six-mile trip for three shillings with an empty drive back, then a three-mile fare with luggage, then a one-shilling return: eighteen miles for six shillings. That horse still owes three shillings, and the afternoon horse nine, before Sam earns anything for his six children.
evidence: now that makes eighteen miles for the horse and six shillings for me
nine shillings for the afternoon horse before I touch a penny

questions.prompt: The Governor says Sam and his horse look fit for the police station. Whom does Sam say the police should go after instead? Why does he say a man “must put your wife and children before the horse”?
facilitatorNotes: The masters who charge so much for cab and horses, and whoever fixed the fares so low. If he does not drive the tired horse with the whip, his children go hungry; the system leaves him no good choice. He insists he does not ill-use the horse for its own sake.
evidence: it ought to be with the masters who charge us so much, or with the fares that are fixed so low
you must put your wife and children before the horse

questions.prompt: “You’ve beaten me, Sam.” What makes the Governor change his mind, and what does he still ask Sam to do?
facilitatorNotes: He admits Sam’s account is all true; he cannot say who could mend it. What moved him was the look in the horse’s eye. He still asks Sam to speak kindly to the horse, because a kind word is something even a poor man can give.
evidence: You've beaten me, Sam
It is hard lines for man, and it's hard lines for beast
Sometimes a kind word is all we can give 'em

questions.prompt: Sam’s last words are about Sundays, and the Governor says, “this is a warning for us.” What is the warning, and who besides the cabmen might Sewell want to hear it?
facilitatorNotes: Endless hours with no day of rest wore out the man as surely as the horse; the cabmen may go the same way. Sewell also aims the warning at readers: passengers who count every penny and cram luggage inside, owners like Skinner, and those who fix the fares. Some may read it more narrowly, as a warning to look after one’s health; the chapter supports both.
evidence: I never had a Sunday's rest
this is a warning for us

readings.title: Black Beauty: An Old War Horse (Chapter XXXIV, excerpt)
readings.challenge: Listen to a veteran telling his own story, and notice what he says about trust, fear and the purpose of the fighting.
readings.focus: Captain, the old cab horse who shares Black Beauty’s stable, tells how he carried his master in a cavalry charge, and what war looked like from the saddle.
readings.context: Black Beauty (1877) is the only book by the English writer Anna Sewell, who wrote it during her last years of illness and died a few months after it was published. A horse tells his own life story, and Sewell meant it to make people kinder to horses, which in her time pulled almost every cart, cab and carriage. Black Beauty now pulls a London cab for Jerry Barker. His stable-mate Captain was trained as a cavalry horse, for soldiers who fight on horseback, and was shipped with a young officer to the Crimean War (1853–56), fought by Britain, France and Turkey against Russia beside the Black Sea. His last charge is like the Charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava in 1854, when British horsemen rode down a valley straight at the Russian guns. Caparisoned means saddled and equipped; restive means restless; farriers shoe and doctor horses; engagements are battles. Veterans Day, November 11, began as Armistice Day, when the First World War’s fighting stopped in 1918, and now honors everyone who has served.
readings.contentNote: Captain describes soldiers and horses killed and terribly wounded in battle, and the shooting of wounded horses afterward.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XXXIV, “An Old War Horse,” from Black Beauty’s question about the fighting to the end of the chapter; opens “"But what about the fighting?" said I; "was not that worse than anything else?"”; closes “…wicked people, if it was right to go all that way over the sea on purpose to kill them."”.

questions.prompt: Captain says he never felt terror in battle until “one dreadful day.” What kept him from fear before, and what changed?
facilitatorNotes: Trust: while his master sat firm and spoke cheerfully, Captain felt that neither of them could be killed. When his master was struck and fell, he was alone and without a guide, and fear took hold of him for the first time.
evidence: I had such perfect trust in him
then, fear took hold on me, and I trembled as I had never trembled before

questions.prompt: On the morning of the charge, the master smooths a stray lock of Captain’s mane and strokes his neck longer than ever before. Why might Sewell include this small moment? What might the master have been thinking?
facilitatorNotes: It shows the love between rider and horse, and it hints at what is coming: the master seems to sense that this day will be different, perhaps his last. Captain, who knew all his moods, stood still for him. Readers may also see a soldier steadying himself as much as his horse.
evidence: He stroked my neck that morning, more I think, than he had ever done before
We shall have a day of it to-day, Bayard, my beauty

questions.prompt: How many of Captain’s stable came back? What happened to the others, and what does Captain say he will never forget?
facilitatorNotes: About one in four returned. The badly wounded were shot by the farriers; the rest lay dead on the field. He cannot forget the groans and the beseeching eyes of the wounded horses left behind as the survivors galloped past.
evidence: In our stables there was only about one in four that returned.
the beseeching look in their eyes

questions.prompt: Black Beauty has heard war spoken of “as if it was a very fine thing.” What is Captain’s answer? When asked what the war was about, he says that is “more than a horse can understand.” What do you think Sewell wants readers to notice in his last words?
facilitatorNotes: War looks fine only on parade; in battle thousands of brave men and horses are killed or crippled. His last answer sounds simple, but it is pointed: if it was right to sail so far to kill them, the enemy “must have been awfully wicked,” which makes readers ask whether they were. Some take it as a horse’s innocence; others as Sewell’s own doubt about the war. Either way, the veteran who served bravely is also the one who tells the truth about its cost.
evidence: I should think they never saw it
that is more than a horse can understand
if it was right to go all that way over the sea on purpose to kill them
